subject: 👀 Anthropic, CPI, oh my!

Plus: Bankers' bonuses boom | Tuesday, November 10, 2026
   
 
 View in browser 
   
 
   
 Axios Markets By
Emily Peck and Matt Phillips
 · 
Nov 10, 2026
 
 
 🌅 It's Tuesday. Big day ahead. 

 🚨 AI giant Anthropic has set its pricing for a $1 trillion-plus IPO just as the AI trade may — or may not — be getting a bounce back.

 📈📉 And U.S. stock futures are mixed this morning after Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller said he supports an interest rate hike in December — as much as a half point. The size of the increase would depend in part on the October inflation data due out later this morning.

 👀 Beleaguered AI cloud provider CoreWeave reports earnings after the close.

 Today, Matt looks at yesterday's wild swing for tech stocks. This time, to the upside. Plus, Emily has new details about this year's Wall Street bonuses. (Hint: more good news for the wealthy.)

 🇺🇸 A quick programming note: We'll be off tomorrow in observance of Veterans Day. To all veterans, thank you for your service. We'll see you Thursday!

 OK, let's get into it! In 1,088 words, a 4-minute read. 


 
   
   
 
1 big thing: AIl in AI, but 1
 
 By Matt Phillips 
   
 
 Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios The AI trade has regained momentum despite — or maybe because of — Nvidia's struggles following the weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang.

 The big picture: Yesterday's sudden burst of exuberance for AI was the latest wide swing for a market upended by last week's "blue tsunami" in the midterm elections and the threat it could pose to the data center boom. 

 By the numbers: The Nasdaq 100 index of large-cap technology shares soared 3.4%, its biggest daily jump since late March and its second-best showing of the year.

 Zoom in: Stocks romped across the AI ecosystem — well, with one important exception. 

 Pick-and-shovel plays, such as engineering and construction companies, and makers of data center inputs like fiber-optic cables, servers and data storage devices soared. The companies that build and lease out data center computing power, known as neoclouds, also jumped. (Those companies had been at the epicenter of recent jitters about financing for the AI boom.) Hyperscalers rose, paced by Meta, which notched a gain of 5.1%. Semiconductors roared, with the SOX index posting its best gain — 6.9% — since late July. Yes, but: The glaring exception to the AI-palooza was its best-known player, Nvidia. 

 Huang 's acknowledgment that he is having an affair with a woman suspected of connections to Chinese intelligence left investors grappling with uncertainty about the CEO's future. The intrigue: Some investors may see Nvidia's pain as potential gain for rivals.

 Broadcom jumped 8.8%, its best day in nearly a year. Advanced Micro Devices soared 13.3%, benefiting also from an upgrade to "Outperform" — effectively, a "buy" recommendation — from Oppenheimer analysts on Sunday. Context: Bullish commentary from Wall Street established the background music for yesterday's big bounce, as analysts urged investors to buy into the market's recent soft patch. 

 "We believe stocks are now clearly in oversold territory," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote in a note. "We believe the market's reaction to the midterms is overdone," wrote Morgan Stanley tech analysts in a note entitled "Buy the Drop: AI Investment Opportunities Post the U.S. Midterms," which it published Sunday night. These analysts could be right. The recent slump has been deep in certain sectors, such as chips. 

 And buying the dip has been a solid strategy in recent years, especially for retail investors . The other side: On the other hand, there may be good reasons such stocks sold off.

 For example, even before the news about the Nvidia CEO or the anti-data center vote at the polls, Wall Street expectations for capital expenditures from hyperscalers had been looking a bit flat. Given that a large percentage of that AI investment is spent on the semiconductors needed to make these computing centers, well, compute, that would seem to be important for tech investors. What's next: Will the stock market's rally be the start of a new phase of AI exuberance? 

 Or is it just an example of Wall Street's proverbial dead cat bounce ?

2. Wall Street bonuses on track for big gains
 
 By Emily Peck 
   
 
 Data: Johnson Associates; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios Wall Street's bankers and traders are set to rake in big increases in year-end bonuses over 2025, say new projections out this morning.

 Why it matters: The AI investment surge has paid off massively on Wall Street, which raced to (for a fee) help hyperscalers, frontier AI firms and other smaller companies issue stock and debt, go public, spin up financing deals and so on.

 The surge in volatility didn't hurt either — traders benefit when markets move around a lot. Plus: Beyond the rich getting richer, the beefy paychecks are crucial to New York state, city budgets and overall economy — juicy payouts typically fuel the real estate and restaurant sectors and state budget coffers.

 By the numbers: The biggest jumps are for the investment bankers who work on equity sales, trading and underwriting, per the third-quarter projections from compensation consulting firm Johnson Associates.

 This group could see an increase of between 20% and 30% or more in bonuses, compared with what they got in 2025. Yes, but: At the bottom of the stack is private equity, where bonus growth could be from zero to 7.5%. 

 And private credit could see bonuses that are flat or decrease by as much as 7.5%. The sector expanded too quickly, sucked in a lot of money and made some questionable loans, says Alan Johnson, the firm's managing director. Next year could be worse. "I don't think the hangover is over yet," he says. How it works: Johnson Associates has been doing this for 25 years and comes up with its closely watched projections by looking at public filings and talking to clients. 

 The intrigue: This is the third consecutive year that bonuses have been significantly higher than the prior year — and this may be a peak, the report says.

 Geopolitical turmoil, rising inflation, higher interest rates and recent market turmoil might mean reduced bonuses in 2027. "The markets and my intuition and everything else going on would say next year is flat to downish. Probably not down a lot, but flat to downish, just because rarely does everything continue to go good all at the same time," Johnson tells Axios. What to watch: AI-driven job cuts are accelerating in the industry. "There's going to be fewer people" in the next couple of years, he says.

 That might mean fewer bankers, but those who keep their jobs may see even more compensation. The bottom line: Some people just stay lucky.
